newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania's opposition defeats ruling leftists.
newsitem.headline: Romania's opposition defeats ruling leftists.

text.p: Romania's centrist opposition has surged to victory in parliamentary elections and should depose ex-communists who have governed since 1989, first results showed on Monday.

Emil Constantinescu's Democratic Convention (CDR) made sure of a central role in the next governing coalition by winning a big lead in both houses of parliament. It will be the first taste of power for the opposition in Romania.

But the country's presidency remained undecided with incumbent Ion Iliescu, a former communist in power since the overthrow of Stalinist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu, holding a three point lead over Constantinescu.
The pair will contest a November 17 run-off, with the outcome uncertain. Foreign observors pronounced the election free and fair, despite worries about poor organisation.

With just over a fifth of the vote counted, the CDR had 30.8 percent in contests for the lower Chamber of Deputies, compared to 20.8 percent for Iliescu's Party of Social Democracy (PDSR). Figures for the Senate were roughly similar.

Convention strategists were ecstatic at the prospect of implementing their "contract with Romania" -- an ambitious plan, if lacking in detail, to speed up reforms to drag post-communist Romania out of its protracted economic crisis.

"After seven years of pseudo-democracy and neo-communist rule, the people realised that a total change was needed," Lucian Hossu Longin, a senior CDR member, told Romanian television without even waiting for results to be confirmed.
"This is a natural reaction because all the promises turned out to be lies and people's lives became worse and worse."
But it was not entirely clear which partners would form a governing coalition or how Iliescu might work with a hostile parliament if he held on to win the run-off.
Romania's nascent financial markets, fearing future instability, refused to react before results became clearer.
Iliescu, who warned against unpredictable lurches if the opposition won power, won 31.8 percent support in the presidential race to Constantinescu's 28.5 percent.

Ex-prime minister Petre Roman lay third with 21.4 percent, votes that will play a pivotal role in the run-off. His Social Democrats (USD) scored 13 percent in the parliamentary vote and appear to hold the balance of power.
Ion Cristoiu, one of Romania's top political analysts predicted a centre-right coalition bringing together the two opposition parties. But he warned it would be fragile.
"If it fails to make the expected changes, it will generate huge disappointment," he said on television.
Roman bitterly attacked Romania's post-Communist plunge into stagnation during the campaign and his economic programme is broadly similar to that of the Convention.
Cooperation between the two parties has been hampered by a personality clash and Roman made no promises on election night.

"There are urgent measures to be undertaken and I only hope that we will be able to form common objectives with the CDR," he said. "We have to be very clear in our future programme to ensure sustainable growth over the next four years."
Clearly disappointed with the outcome, Iliescu tried to exploit opposition differences by suggesting the CDR might be better off building a coalition with his battered PDSR.
The ethnic Hungarian UDMR party, generally unfriendly towards Iliescu, took fourth place with a pivotal six percent.
Romanian nationalist parties look to be the only other political groups scoring strongly enough to beat the three percent threshold for a place in parliament.
